Intel Foundry: How Better Power Delivery Could Unlock More AI Performanceby Daniel Nenni on 11-27-2026 at 6:00 am

Categories: 3D IC, Chiplet, Intel Foundry, Semiconductor

Key takeaways ▼

An AI accelerator can have more transistors, more memory bandwidth, and a faster interconnect, yet still leave performance on the table if its power delivery network cannot keep up. Intel Foundry’s white paper Driving Power Delivery Innovations for the AI Data Center Era makes an optimistic case for what comes next. Engineers can shorten the path electricity takes to the transistors, put more stored charge near the circuits that need it, and move voltage conversion closer to the compute die. Together, those changes could help future accelerators make better use of the power they draw.
The challenge starts with current
AI accelerators operate at low voltages, so supplying more power means delivering more current. Intel’s paper puts package currents in the multi-kiloamp range for highly integrated designs. Resistive losses rise with the square of current, which makes long delivery paths increasingly costly. Sudden jumps in demand can also cause a brief drop in supply voltage. Designers may compensate by raising the operating voltage enough to maintain stability through those dips, increasing energy consumption in the process.
That challenge grows as compute chiplets and high-bandwidth memory share a package. The routing and surface area needed to supply power are also needed for high-speed connections, and each die can have different voltage and current requirements. Intel Foundry’s approach gives designers several places to act, from the silicon itself to the package and the voltage regulator.
Shorter paths and steadier voltage
PowerVia, introduced on Intel 18A, routes power through the back of the die while leaving frontside wiring available for signals. Shorter current paths reduce resistive voltage drop, and separating the two networks eases routing congestion. That gives designers more freedom to improve power delivery and signal routing independently. Intel plans to build on that approach with PowerDirect on Intel 14A.
The paper also describes how to handle the moment an accelerator suddenly needs more current. Capacitors close to the active circuitry supply charge while the regulator catches up. Intel’s Omni MIM uses vertical trenches to fit more capacitance into a given area on the die. Embedded capacitors add charge storage inside the package, where surface space is scarce. EMIB-T, meanwhile, adds vertical paths through the silicon bridge connecting dies, so current can take a more direct route through a densely packed design. These changes matter as packages bring compute and memory closer together and have to supply both within a limited footprint.
Voltage conversion offers another opportunity. Moving the regulator closer to the compute die shortens the distance that low-voltage, high-current power has to travel. Intel’s continuous capacitive voltage regulator, or C2VR, uses capacitors in place of inductors and can be thinned to less than 100 micrometers for potential placement beneath a compute die. Intel reports a 92% peak conversion efficiency for the research design cited in the paper. The placement is as interesting as the efficiency figure. Bringing conversion directly under the load creates a shorter vertical path and helps the regulator respond quickly when demand changes.
Why it matters beyond the package
Data centers have a finite amount of power and cooling capacity to allocate. At the same facility power budget, an accelerator that loses less energy between the voltage regulator and the transistors can leave more of that budget available for computation. Lower distribution losses also mean less heat from the power delivery network itself. Over many accelerators, even modest gains can affect how much compute fits within a rack’s electrical and thermal limits. The size of those gains will depend on the accelerator, its workload, and how the package is built.
The foundry opportunity is to give chip designers a choice about where to make those gains. A high-current logic die may benefit most from backside delivery. A package crowded with memory and chiplets may have more to gain from embedded capacitors or a bridge that carries power vertically. A stacked design could benefit from placing a regulator directly beneath the compute die. Having those options makes power delivery a design decision architects can make alongside transistor technology, memory bandwidth, and packaging. For AI and high-performance computing, that opens a path to higher performance by getting more useful work out of the power already available.
Source:  Intel Foundry, Driving Power Delivery Innovations for the AI Data Center Era.
